summary: Describes how the Border Gateway Protocol is applied in the Internet, as a companion to RFC 1163. Together they specify an inter-autonomous system routing protocol. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1268.

eli5.summary: This is the how-to for using the early network-to-network road map system on the real Internet.

subtitle: How early BGP was meant to be used between autonomous systems: policy, path choice and living alongside interior routing.

tldr.problem: RFC 1163 defines the Border Gateway Protocol, but operators also need to know how to use it: how networks connect, how to express routing policy, and how BGP fits with the routing protocol inside each network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a topology model of autonomous systems, shows how path preferences and redistribution rules express policy, sketches a policy language, and lists ways to keep BGP and an interior gateway protocol consistent.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1268, so it describes the first generation of BGP practice, not current guidance.

today: RFC 1164 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1268, so it records early BGP practice and is not current guidance. It was issued as a Proposed Standard together with RFC 1163.

sections.title: Purpose and Setting
sections.content:
This memo is a companion to RFC 1163, which defines the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Together they define a Proposed Standard for routing between autonomous systems. BGP carries enough reachability information to detect routing loops and to enforce decisions based on performance preference and the policy constraints outlined in RFC 1104.

The memo treats the Internet as a collection of arbitrarily connected Autonomous Systems (ASs). An AS is run by a single administration and presents one coherent interior routing plan to the outside, even if it uses several interior gateway protocols (IGPs) and sets of metrics inside. From the outside, an AS is monolithic: reachability to directly connected networks must be the same from all of its border gateways.
sections.eli5: Each big network is like a country with its own rules inside. This booklet explains how those countries talk to their neighbors about which roads they can reach.

sections.title: The Topological Model and AS Types
sections.content:
The model is a graph whose nodes are ASs and whose edges are connections. A connection means two things: a physical connection (a shared network where each AS has at least one border gateway) and a BGP connection (a BGP session between BGP speakers on that same shared network). Only the AS's border gateways on that shared network may appear in NEXT_HOP attributes of Update messages.

Traffic that starts or ends in an AS is local traffic; everything else is transit traffic, and controlling transit traffic is a major goal of BGP usage. That gives three kinds of AS:

  • Stub AS: a single connection to another AS, carrying only local traffic.
  • Multihomed AS: more than one connection, but refuses to carry transit traffic.
  • Transit AS: more than one connection and, under policy restrictions, carries both transit and local traffic.

Because a full AS path suppresses routing loops and removes the count-to-infinity problem of some distance vector algorithms, BGP puts no topological restrictions on how ASs interconnect.
sections.eli5: A town with one road out is a stub. A town with two roads that never lets outsiders drive through is multihomed. A town that lets through-traffic pass is a transit town.

sections.title: BGP in the Internet
sections.content:
To limit the impact on the existing Internet, stub and multihomed ASs need not run BGP. They may use another protocol such as EGP to exchange reachability with transit ASs, which then tag that information as learned via EGP or another method. BGP may still be used by stub and multihomed ASs, which would give better bandwidth and performance than some current protocols and reduce the need for defaults.

Between ASs only BGP carries routing information, while inside an AS a combination of BGP and an IGP does the job. BGP neighbors may be in different ASs (External BGP, which should run over a shared common network, since using BGP across an intervening AS invalidates the AS path) or in the same AS (Internal BGP). All BGP gateways of one AS must present a consistent image of the AS to the outside and apply consistent policy constraints.
sections.eli5: Small towns can keep using the old way of talking to the big towns. Big towns use the new way and also have to keep their own streets and highways telling the same story.

sections.title: Policy and Path Selection
sections.content:
Policies come from the AS administration and are given to BGP as configuration; they are not encoded in the protocol. They act in two ways: by affecting which path is selected from several alternatives, and by controlling redistribution of routes. Examples include refusing to be a transit AS, allowing only a chosen set of ASs to use it as transit, preferring shorter AS paths, and preferring internal over external routes. Non-technical policy typically overrides performance. Ties must be resolved deterministically.

A fundamental rule is that an AS advertises to its neighbors only the routes that it uses. This fits the hop-by-hop paradigm, so BGP cannot express policies that need source routing, but it can support any policy that fits hop-by-hop routing.

Each speaker keeps all feasible paths but advertises only the primary one. Paths are ranked by a degree of preference, which can come from criteria such as AS count, presence of particular ASs, path origin (a path that is BGP the whole way is generally better than one partly learned via EGP), AS path subsets, link stability (to be used very carefully), and policy. Compound criteria that mix such measures should be used with extreme caution.
sections.eli5: Each town keeps a list of every road to a faraway place but tells its neighbors about only its favorite. It picks favorites by things like how many towns it passes through, and by its own rules about who it likes.

sections.title: A Policy Configuration Language
sections.content:
The memo offers one possible syntax for writing AS path policies, noting that other syntaxes are not precluded. An AS path is matched against patterns written as regular expressions over AS numbers, using operators for any AS, zero or more repetitions, one or more repetitions, an optional element, alternation, grouping and explicit repeat counts.

Each policy statement has the form <network-list> <AS-path> <origin> <distribution-list> = <degree of preference>. The origin is IGP, EGP, INCOMPLETE or ANY. The distribution list names the neighbor ASs that may receive the route. A degree of preference of REJECT means the route is not used; otherwise higher values are preferred. Two built-in functions exist: PathLength() and PathWeight(), the latter summing per-AS weights with a mandatory default weight.

Matching stops at the first successful match, so terms should go from more specific to more general. The memo works through examples for a five-AS topology, such as a transit backbone with a simple permissive policy, a stub that does not trust its transit provider and adds its own filter, and a multihomed AS that prefers one provider with another as backup.
sections.eli5: The language is a list of rules like: if a route comes from these towns, give it this many points and tell these neighbors. The first rule that fits wins, so the pickiest rules go first.

sections.title: Working with the Interior Gateway Protocol
sections.content:
Transit traffic crosses both interior gateways (IGP only) and border gateways (IGP and BGP). Because changes spread at different rates, there can be a window when a border gateway has new BGP information but the IGP cannot yet route transit traffic to the exit gateway, producing incorrect routing or "black holes". The rule of thumb: interior routing should converge on the proper exit gateway before the route is advertised to other ASs.

Three methods are described:

  • Carry BGP information in the IGP, if the IGP supports complete flooding and one-pass convergence. The IGP must not interpret the data.
  • Tagged IGP: exterior routes carry a tag that identifies the exit gateway. A gateway must pass on unreachability at once, but may announce a reachable network externally only when it has an IGP route and the IGP and BGP tags are identical.
  • Encapsulation: transit traffic is wrapped in an IP datagram addressed to the exit gateway named in the "gateway" field of the Update message, so no BGP and IGP synchronization is needed.

For IGPs that can neither carry BGP data nor tag routes (RIP is the example), a holddown time is needed before announcing. If IGP convergence is faster than some small value X, which should probably be under one second, the problem can be ignored.
sections.eli5: Before a town tells the outside world "you can get to that place through our east gate", it should make sure its own streets already point people to that gate. Otherwise visitors get lost.
